paras: The attempted lynching of Sisco took place in Rockland County, New York, on August 20, 1905, when crowds threatened to lynch a Black prisoner named Sisco at Haverstraw and then went to the New City jail intending to hang him. Sisco was held as the suspected companion of a man named Brown, accused of shooting two Haverstraw policemen the night before, and the crowds failed to reach him. Only the New-York Tribune reported the lynching threats in detail; a wire story printed as far away as Nebraska carried the shooting and Sisco's capture without the mob.

Haverstraw's brickyards employed Black laborers, some of whom, the Tribune said, got drunk after their Saturday pay and engaged in shooting affrays. According to the Tribune, Patrolmen John Cahill, William Springstead and Call set out on the night of August 19 to disarm drunken laborers and stopped two Black men on the road. One of them, known as "Steamboat" Brown, was said to have declared that "no white man could take away his gun" before shooting Cahill dead and wounding Springstead, while Call ran for help.

The Sun's first report, from Nyack, said instead that the officers were driving two Black women prisoners, Mary Brown and Maud Sicco, to the New City jail when two men jumped from the bushes and fired. It did not name the assailants but said they were believed to be "Southern negroes" who had lived with the women near the brickyards.

Several hundred white men armed themselves and searched the woods and hills around Haverstraw. On August 20 Constable Towers of Garnersville, with the Newburgh police, arrested Sisco, a "colored man" seen jumping from a train at Cornwall and believed to be Brown's companion. He reportedly told contradictory stories and was taken to Haverstraw for Call to identify.

Word of his arrival spread quickly, and a crowd of several hundred men gathered, threatening to lynch him. District Attorney Lee of Rockland County told the crowd that the law would punish Cahill's killer; the rest of his remarks is illegible in the printed report. Fearing violence, the police moved Sisco to the jail at New City. That night more than two hundred men went to New City declaring that they would take him from the jail and hang him, but they failed to reach him and went home.

The Rockland County supervisors and Haverstraw citizens each offered $1,000 for the capture of Cahill's killer. Police later arrested other suspects: Jesse Crisfield, a Black waiter, in New York on August 24, and Reuben Clark, with Ashley Drew held as a witness, at Brunswick, Georgia, on September 1. None of these reports mentions Sisco, and no account of charges against him or of action against the crowds was found.
By late August Haverstraw had sworn in six special policemen, and two priests of St. Peter's Church were campaigning against saloons they blamed for violence by Black residents.

The Tribune's special dispatch, headed "Lynching Plans Fail" and "Haverstraw Mob Out," was the only detailed account of the threats against Sisco. It called Brown "the negro murderer" and the crowd "angry citizens," praised the two officers' "courage to make arrests in the brickyards," and did not criticize the crowds. The Tribune's news digest reduced the episode to one sentence, which the New Haven Union reprinted almost verbatim the same day.

A wire story ran the shooting under headlines such as "Negro Shoots Two Policemen" and "Fatal Fight with Negroes" in Nebraska, Virginia and South Dakota. The same brief, naming Sisco as a captured companion, appeared in Iowa on August 24 and in Wyoming on September 22.

Later New York coverage turned to Haverstraw's Black workers, with the Tribune's "Negroes Unrestrained" saying about 2,000 of them had "terrorized the whole town." All of the coverage found came from white papers; no report of the episode appeared in the Black press.

The first accounts of the shooting disagreed on its occasion: the Sun described a rescue of women prisoners, the Tribune and wire an attempt to disarm drunken laborers. The Sun placed Springstead's wound in the thigh and expected him to recover; the Tribune placed it in the stomach and said he probably could not live.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Sisco
bases: Crowds of several hundred and then more than two hundred men threatened to lynch Sisco and went to the New City jail to take him out and hang him, but failed (A2, A3).

The crowds, acting without authority and in response to the shooting of a policeman, sought to hang Sisco, but no one was killed by them (A2); the standard definition requires a killing, so this was an attempted lynching.

Only the New-York Tribune reports the lynching threats and the march on the New City jail (A2); its digest (A3) and the New Haven Union copy (A4) are not independent, while the wire (A6, A7) confirms only Sisco's capture.

accounts.label: Tribune special correspondent
accounts.gist: Police stopping armed drunken laborers were shot by Brown; Sisco, caught as his companion, nearly was lynched at Haverstraw and a second crowd failed to get him from New City jail.

accounts.label: Sun dispatch from Nyack
accounts.gist: Two unnamed Black men jumped from the bushes and shot the officers to free two Black women prisoners being driven to New City jail.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Brown shot the officers while they tried to disperse drinking Black men near the brickyard; a companion, Sisco, was captured; no mention of a mob.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'Lynching Plans Fail / Haverstraw Mob Out', called the crowd 'angry citizens' and Brown 'the negro murderer', praised the officers, and offered no criticism of the crowds.
Wire papers ran the shooting as 'Negro Shoots Two Policemen' or 'Fatal Fight with Negroes' and omitted the lynching threats.
Follow-ups in the Sun and Tribune portrayed Haverstraw's Black brickyard workers as a 'lawless negro element' that had 'terrorized the whole town', without mention of the mob.
